slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code defines and registers a TinyMCE plugin that initializes a jQuery-based spellchecker using a web service at "/src/webservices/php/SpellChecker.php", enabling spellchecking functionality within the editor without external data transmission.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code defines a TinyMCE plugin that integrates a jQuery-based spellchecker using a local web service endpoint (/src/webservices/php/SpellChecker.php). It does not perform any remote script injection, dynamic fetching of external malicious payloads, clipboard monitoring, or credential theft. The plugin's behavior is consistent with legitimate spellchecking functionality within a web editor. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks key indicators such as loading remote attacker-controlled scripts, injecting phishing forms, or manipulating sensitive user data. The code is straightforward, unobfuscated, and does not exhibit suspicious API usage or intent.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
key_indicators: Injection of remote scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Phony deprecation warnings in console output to mislead users
Use of outdated or deprecated library versions
Chaining to further malicious payloads via dynamic script loading

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, on page load or script execution

package_info.package_versions: 8.0.0 (and dozens of others, see report for full list)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.

attack_chain.action: User installs a malicious npm package containing a trojanized jQuery file (or similar).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the project and loaded in the browser.

attack_chain.action: Trojanized jQuery is loaded and used in the web application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious prototype function (end) is available in the global jQuery object.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls fadeTo or end (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious end function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is serialized and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains.

attack_chain.action: Injected scripts (from icons.js/min.js) load additional remote payloads (e.g., slim.js) from jsDelivr, which may contain further trojanized code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and further compromise of the web application.

behavioral_signatures: Modification of jQuery prototype functions (especially end) to perform network requests
Exfiltration of serialized form data via AJAX to external domains
Dynamic injection of remote scripts from non-standard or outdated sources
Presence of phony deprecation warnings in console output
file_indicators: jquery.min.js, registration.min.js, icon.min.js, fontawesome.js, slim.js, all-min.js (with non-standard or unexpected content)
Presence of termux.properties, npm cache, or npm logs in package tarballs
network_indicators: Requests to domains such as *.truex.biz.id, *.hanznesia.my.id, *.api-system.engineer, *.jsdelivr.net/gh/indexsc/libs/slim.js, and other listed campaign domains
AJAX GET requests with hex-encoded form data in query parameters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript dependencies for modifications to core library prototype functions (e.g., jQuery.fn.end). Flag any code that serializes and exfiltrates form data to external domains. Monitor for dynamic script injection from non-standard or outdated sources, and alert on requests to known campaign domains. Review package contents for unexpected files (e.g., termux.properties, npm logs) and non-standard file naming patterns. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify supply chain attacks.

matched_knowledge.source_package: standforusz, react-vuejs, tetusdgsudgs, jqueryoffline, vueofflinez, jquerydownloadnew (npm)

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
<script src="jquery.js"></script>
// jquery.js fetches jquery.min.js from CDN, which then fetches DEMO.txt and writes its content (fake login form) to the document.
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads jquery.js, which fetches additional JavaScript and text files from a remote CDN, reads DEMO.txt containing a fake Microsoft login form, injects the form into the DOM, and enables credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and dynamically injecting remote content to display a credential harvesting form is a well-known phishing technique, especially when the content mimics Microsoft login pages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject fake login forms or exfiltrate user credentials, nor should they fetch and execute remote scripts without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic content loading is common for legitimate widgets or analytics, but not for credential forms or authentication interfaces.
key_indicators: Dynamic fetching of remote scripts and text files
Injection of fake Microsoft login forms into the DOM
Credential exfiltration logic targeting attacker infrastructure
Use of misleading file names (e.g., jquery.js) to mimic legitimate libraries

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a malicious HTML attachment is opened in the browser)
execution_context.file_location: jquery.js (from standforusz package, used in phishing email attachments)

The packages are distributed via npm and are designed to be included in phishing email attachments or as supply chain implants in web applications.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that contain obfuscated JavaScript, especially in main entry points or files named after popular libraries (e.g., jquery.js). Detect network traffic to known malicious domains or IPs (ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz, 137.184.153.238) and monitor for HTTP POST requests with credential data to these endpoints. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify code that disables browser inspection tools or dynamically injects login forms. Correlate file, behavioral, and network indicators to identify and block malicious packages before they are executed.

matched_knowledge.source_package: yfinacne (and >450 other typosquats, e.g., vyper, cryptocompare, etc.) (pypi)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the Python code writes this JavaScript to a browser extension file, which, when loaded by the browser, monitors the clipboard every second, detects cryptocurrency wallet addresses using regex patterns, and replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses, resulting in silent redirection of cryptocurrency transactions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The JavaScript code is designed to be deployed as a browser extension without user consent and actively manipulates clipboard contents to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with those controlled by the attacker. This is a direct attempt to steal funds by hijacking user transactions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not install browser extensions or manipulate clipboard data for the purpose of redirecting sensitive information such as cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Clipboard monitoring may be used in accessibility or productivity tools, but not for the silent replacement of sensitive data with attacker-controlled values.
key_indicators: Writes browser extension files containing clipboard monitoring logic
Uses regular expressions to detect multiple cryptocurrency wallet formats
Hardcoded attacker-controlled wallet addresses for multiple cryptocurrencies
Automated clipboard replacement and copy operations

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
// Heavily obfuscated JavaScript storing VirusTotal API keys
var _0xabc=['...obfuscated string...'];(function(_0xdef,_0x123){...})(_0xabc,0x1a2b3);
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code loads a heavily obfuscated string from 'src/secret.js', decodes it using a simple reversible algorithm, and exposes the VirusTotal API keys for use by other parts of the package.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code employs heavy obfuscation to hide static VirusTotal API keys, a technique frequently used by malware authors to conceal secrets or malicious payloads from static analysis and detection tools.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should never store sensitive API keys directly in source code, especially not in an obfuscated form. Proper secret management requires using environment variables or secure secret management solutions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in legitimate software to protect proprietary algorithms or reduce code size, but it is not appropriate for hiding static API keys or secrets.
key_indicators: Presence of a file named 'secret.js' in the source directory
Heavily obfuscated JavaScript code using array and function wrappers
Static storage of VirusTotal API keys in package code
Decoding logic that reveals sensitive information at import-time

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a heavily obfuscated JavaScript file ('src/secret.js') that statically stores VirusTotal API keys using simple, reversible obfuscation. This practice is a significant security risk, as it exposes sensitive credentials to anyone who inspects or decodes the package. The use of obfuscation to conceal static secrets is a common tactic among malicious packages, and legitimate packages should never embed API keys in code, especially in an obfuscated form.

attack_chain.action: Obfuscated JavaScript code in 'src/secret.js' is loaded and executed at import-time, decoding and exposing the VirusTotal API keys for use by the package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential misuse of the exposed VirusTotal API keys by anyone who inspects or decodes the package, leading to abuse, quota exhaustion, or compromise of the associated VirusTotal account.

behavioral_signatures: Heavily obfuscated JavaScript files present in npm packages, especially in files named 'secret.js'
Static API keys or secrets stored in obfuscated code and decoded at runtime
Obfuscated code that, when executed, reveals sensitive information such as VirusTotal API keys
file_indicators: Any file with 'secret' in the filename containing obfuscated JavaScript code
network_indicators: Unusual or unauthorized use of VirusTotal API endpoints originating from package consumers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should inspect npm packages for files named 'secret.js' or similar, and analyze their contents for obfuscated code patterns (e.g., array-based string obfuscation, self-invoking decoding functions). Static analysis should attempt to decode obfuscated strings to identify embedded API keys or secrets. Flag any package that statically stores and obfuscates sensitive information. Monitor for anomalous or excessive use of VirusTotal API keys from consumers of the package.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Boom! Mobile website (boom[.]us) Magecart skimmer (N/A (injected JavaScript on e-commerce website))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At page load, the code loads an external JavaScript skimmer from a Base64-encoded URL, executes it in the context of the checkout page, and enables the interception of payment form data for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading an external script from a Base64-encoded URL is a deliberate obfuscation technique to evade static detection and code review. The script source is not associated with the legitimate business and points to a suspicious, attacker-controlled domain.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate e-commerce sites should only load scripts from trusted, first-party, or well-known third-party sources. The use of Base64-encoded script sources and unrecognized domains is not expected in production environments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Base64-encoded script URLs are almost never used in legitimate production e-commerce environments, as they complicate maintenance and security reviews.
key_indicators: Base64-encoded external script source in <script> tag
Script loaded from a domain not associated with the business (e.g., google-standard[.]com)
Script injection on sensitive payment or checkout pages

execution_context.trigger: At page load (when user accesses the payment/checkout page)
execution_context.file_location: Injected inline in HTML or as an external script reference (e.g., <script> tag on payment page)

package_info.why_malicious: The website was compromised by attackers who injected a malicious JavaScript skimmer. This script intercepts and exfiltrates payment card and private data entered by customers during checkout to attacker-controlled domains, constituting a classic Magecart attack targeting e-commerce transactions.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains access to the website and injects a malicious script tag with a Base64-encoded external source into the payment or checkout page.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious skimmer script is loaded and executed in the context of the checkout page.

attack_chain.action: The external skimmer script executes, hooks into the payment form's submit event, and collects user-entered payment and personal data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Collected payment and personal data is prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: The skimmer script sends the stolen payment and personal data to attacker-controlled domains via HTTPS POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen credit card and personal information from compromised customers.

behavioral_signatures: Inline or external scripts loaded from non-standard, suspicious, or recently registered domains on payment or checkout pages
Base64-encoded script sources in HTML <script> tags
JavaScript code that hooks form submission events and sends collected data to external domains
file_indicators: References to domains such as google-standard[.]com, bing-analytics[.]com, google-money[.]com in script sources
Unexpected or unauthorized script tags present on payment or checkout pages
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to domains like google-standard[.]com, bing-analytics[.]com, google-money[.]com during checkout or payment form submission
Unusual network traffic to recently registered or non-canonical domains originating from payment pages
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for <script> tags in HTML that load resources from suspicious or encoded sources, especially on payment or checkout pages. Inspect JavaScript for event listeners on forms that collect and send data to external domains. Use network monitoring to detect POST requests to known skimmer domains. Flag any new or unrecognized domains in script sources or network traffic, particularly those registered recently or not associated with the business. Correlate script injection events with anomalous network activity to identify active skimming.
